source.title: Preference Optimization for Reasoning with Pseudo Feedback
source.authors: Fangkai Jiao; Geyang Guo; Xingxing Zhang; Nancy F. Chen; Shafiq R. Joty; Furu Wei

page_placements.theme: Self-improvement and self-labelling without a weaker supervisor

record.file_problem: None; the full paper is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports outcomes from pseudo-feedback preference training, but does not test weak-to-strong generalization as defined in the claim: it does not compare a strong student with a weaker labeling supervisor or measure PGR.
record.gate_note: The paper reports benchmark gains from training with GPT-4o-generated or self-consistency pseudo feedback. These results are related to weak supervision, but the supervisors are not compared as weaker models against stronger students, and no strong-model true-label ceiling or PGR is reported. The results are recorded as fitting no listed claim version.
record.test_reason: The paper trains 7–8B models by DPO on pseudo feedback from a stronger model (GPT-4o) or from the policy's own self-consistency. No weaker model supervises a stronger student, and there is no weak-supervisor baseline, true-label strong ceiling or PGR. Burns et al. is cited only as motivation, in the introduction. The record's relation 'tests' contradicts its own T6 tranche; corrected to cites_only.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that pseudo feedback from frontier LLMs (GPT-4o) and from self-consistency, including a new test-case-level self-consistency for code, improves DPO-based math and code results over SFT. They also find iterative training gives further gains that saturate.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses DPO with pseudo answers or test cases from GPT-4o or the policy model itself. It does not use the weak-to-strong setup or PGR measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports variation by feedback source, training iteration, prompt set, and benchmark; some code benchmarks do not improve further with additional xCodeEval data.

fits_no_version.finding: DPO on pseudo feedback (GPT-4o answers, or the policy's own self-consistency over synthetic test cases) raises math and code benchmark scores over SFT. On APPs, self-consistency pseudo test cases match or beat ground-truth test cases (17.4 vs 16.9).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Self-improvement via preference optimization on pseudo feedback (self-consistency or frontier-LLM labels) improves LLM reasoning over SFT baselines without human labels.

record.problems: The paper does not report uncertainty estimates for the listed results and does not compare the student against the model producing its pseudo labels or report a true-label ceiling.
record.rows_left_out: Other iterations, benchmark scores, DPO/pDPO comparisons, and analyses are not separately listed; they concern the same pseudo-feedback training method and do not add a weak-supervisor comparison or PGR result.

untested.parts: Whether a strong student trained on a weaker model's labels beats that supervisor; PGR. The supervisors here are stronger (GPT-4o) or the model itself.
Training changes that raise PGR over naive weak-to-strong fine-tuning.
How PGR varies with supervisor or student size, task, or representations.
Exploitation of unchecked weak-supervisor errors, PGR under distribution shift, or effects of error similarity.
Theoretical conditions for a student to beat its supervisor.

record.verdict_notes: Not a weak-to-strong study. Where an external supervisor is used, it (GPT-4o) is stronger than the student, so the setup is distillation or self-training, not weak supervision of a strong model. The text calls the policy models 'weaker' only when reporting their test-case quality (62.68% vs GPT-4o's 82.41%); this is not a weak-to-strong comparison. Several row baselines and iteration labels were misread from Table 1 and Table 3 (see row_fixes).

versions.untested_parts: Whether the strong student beats a weaker labeling supervisor; PGR and a true-label strong-model ceiling.
Whether auxiliary confidence loss, weak-supervisor ensembling, or loss variants raise PGR over naive weak-to-strong fine-tuning.
How PGR varies with supervisor or student size, task, or representations.
Supervisor-checking failures, distribution shift effects on PGR, or error similarity effects.
Theoretical conditions for a student to beat its supervisor.
Weak-to-strong generalization outside language, including vision.
